introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: three hours.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will be penalised.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised composition will be severely sanctioned.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION C - PRESCRIBED TEXTS (20 Marks)**

Answer ONE question only.

1. Read the following extract from Alex La Guma's *A Walk in the Night* and answer the questions below it.

*(The numbers in square brackets are the line numbers printed in the paper; the printed lines are kept as in the paper.)*

Joe was short and his face had an ***ageless*** quality about it under the ***grime,*** like something valuable
forgotten in a junk shop. He had the soft brown eyes of a dog, and the smell of a mixture of sweat, slept-in
clothes and seaweed. His trousers had ***gone at the cuffs*** and knees, the rents held together with pins and
pieces of string, and so stained and spotted that the original could not have been guessed at. Over the trousers
he wore an ***ancient*** raincoat that reached almost to his ankles, the sleeves torn loose at the shoulders, the [5]
body hanging in ribbons, the front pinned together over his filthy vest. His shoes were worn beyond
recognition.

Nobody knew where Joe came from, or anything about him. He just seemed to have happened,
appearing in the District like a cockroach emerging through a floorboard. Most of the time he wandered
around the harbour gathering fish discarded by fishermen and anglers, or along the beaches of the coast,
picking limpets and mussels. He had a strange passion for things that came from the sea. [10]
incertitudes: Section C question 1 : l'extrait de Alex La Guma, A Walk in the Night, est recopie en entier avec ses mots en gras italique (ageless, grime, gone at the cuffs, ancient) et ses numeros de ligne imprimes. Les reperes imprimes « 5 » (en face de la 5e ligne) et « 10 » (en face de la derniere ligne, soit la 11e ligne imprimee, la ligne vide du changement de paragraphe n'etant pas comptee comme les autres) sont gardes tels quels entre crochets ; les renvois du sujet (L1, L3, L5) correspondent bien aux lignes imprimees 1, 3 et 5.
Points imprimes : (a) 4 marks (le « (4 marks) » est imprime a droite de l'item (iv)), (b) 4, (c) 2, (d) 4, (e) 6, soit 20 ; aucun ecart avec le total de 20 marks de la section.

Corrige de methode : oeuvre non disponible. Seules les sous-questions (a), (b), (c) et (d) se traitent a partir du passage imprime ; la sous-question (e) (la pauvrete dans deux autres oeuvres au programme) exige la connaissance d'oeuvres que je n'ai pas : le corrige donne un plan et des criteres, sans detail d'intrigue.

Sous-question (c) : la reponse attendue par le jury n'est pas imprimee ; la reponse modele met le verbe principal au present perfect (« has had ») et laisse le verbe de la subordonnee au present ou au present perfect, les deux etant acceptables.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**a.** Give the meaning in context of the following words or expressions:

(i) "... *ageless*" (L1)

(ii) "... *grime*" (L1)

(iii) "... *gone at the cuffs*" (L3)

(iv) "... *ancient*" (L5)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (1 mark each)**

1. **ageless** (L1): having no visible age, neither young nor old; the dirt and wear on Joe's face make it impossible to say how old he is.
2. **grime** (L1): thick, ingrained dirt, filth that has settled on the skin over a long time.
3. **gone at the cuffs** (L3): worn out and frayed at the bottom edges of the trouser legs (the cuffs), the cloth torn and ragged.
4. **ancient** (L5): very old and worn out; the raincoat is so old that it is out of date and falling to pieces (the next words, "torn loose" and "hanging in ribbons", confirm the sense).

**Method.** "In context" means that the meaning must fit the sentence: give a synonym or a short explanation, and tie it to the picture of poverty that the writer is building. A bare dictionary definition that does not fit the passage loses the mark.
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: **b.** Briefly say what you consider to be the message in the extract.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (4 marks)**

The extract presents Joe as a man at the very bottom of society: dirty, dressed in rags, without a known origin and living on what the sea throws away. The message is that poverty reduces a human being to something people look past: Joe is treated like an object that "just seemed to have happened", and nobody knows or asks anything about him. At the same time the writer asks the reader for sympathy: under the grime Joe's face has an "ageless quality", "like something valuable forgotten in a junk shop", and he has the "soft brown eyes of a dog". So the passage condemns a society that neglects its poor and reminds us that the outcast has value and dignity.

**Marking.** One mark each for: (1) the idea of poverty and social neglect; (2) a piece of evidence (rags, filth, nameless origin, scavenging); (3) the contrast between his appearance and his hidden worth; (4) the writer's attitude (sympathy and criticism of indifference). The message is drawn from the extract alone, which is all the paper prints.
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown: **c.** Put the last sentence of the passage in the present perfect tense.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (2 marks)**

Original: *He had a strange passion for things that came from the sea.*

Present perfect: **He has had a strange passion for things that come from the sea.**

**Marking.** One mark for the main verb in the present perfect ("has had", from "had") and one mark for a correct rest of the sentence. The relative clause may stay in the present ("things that come from the sea") or take the present perfect ("things that have come from the sea"); both are grammatically correct, and the sentence must remain a single, error-free sentence.

**Common mistake.** Writing "He have had" or "He has have", or changing the sense by dropping "strange".

questions.enonce_markdown: **d.** What image of Joe do you cut from the passage?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (4 marks)**

The passage cuts the image of a **destitute, pitiable tramp**. He is dirty and smelly ("grime", "the smell of a mixture of sweat, slept-in clothes and seaweed"). His clothes are rags held together with "pins and pieces of string", an "ancient raincoat" "hanging in ribbons" and shoes "worn beyond recognition". He is a **rootless outsider**: "Nobody knew where Joe came from", and he appears "like a cockroach emerging through a floorboard", an image of something unwanted and lowly. He is also a **lonely scavenger** who gathers discarded fish and shellfish along the coast, with an odd "passion" for the sea. Yet there is a gentler side: his "soft brown eyes of a dog" and the "something valuable forgotten in a junk shop" suggest an innocent and neglected person who deserves pity.

**Marking.** One mark per distinct point (dirty and ragged; rootless and unknown; scavenger who lives on the margins; pitiable but valuable), each supported by a short quotation from the passage.
themes: A Level English - figures of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: **e.** How is the idea of poverty as used in this passage illustrated in any two other prescribed texts?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Corrige de methode (the two other texts are not available for this model answer)**

The question asks for a comparison: the idea of poverty seen in the extract (rags, dirt, hunger, social neglect, a person nobody notices) must be traced in TWO other prescribed texts. Use this plan (about 3 marks per text, 6 marks in all):

1. **Link** (one sentence): recall how the extract shows poverty (Joe's clothes, smell, lonely scavenging).
2. **First text**: name the text and its writer; identify one character or situation that shows poverty (lack of food, money, home or opportunity); give one precise example (an event, a description, a line you remember); say HOW the writer shows it (description, setting, dialogue, other characters' attitudes, narrative tone); say what the writer wants us to feel or think (pity, anger, criticism of society).
3. **Second text**: the same four steps, with a different kind of poverty if possible (material poverty, poverty of opportunity, poverty caused by injustice or by greed).
4. **Conclusion** (one or two lines): compare with Joe; what do the writers have in common in their treatment of poverty?

**Marking.** The marks go to the choice of two other texts (not the extract), accurate, specific examples, and an explanation of how the writer illustrates poverty, not to a retelling of the plot.
